```{python}
#| echo: false
import sys, pathlib
sys.path.insert(0, str(pathlib.Path.cwd() / "src"))
from lectures import plotting, datasets
from lectures.plotting import INK, COOL, WARM, CRASH, despine, annotate_box
from rbig import AnnealedRBIG
from lectures.measures import cocrash_fraction
plotting.set_style("notes")
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.stats import multivariate_t
import einx                      # linear algebra with the axes spelled out
from jaxtyping import Float      # shape annotations: Float[Array, "n_days 2"]

Array = np.ndarray
GREEN = plotting.PALETTE["green"]
PURPLE = plotting.PALETTE["purple"]
```

The [transformation rule](02-probability-under-transformation.qmd) ended at a
fork: when the function bends and the inputs are wide, the only honest way to
carry uncertainty forward is to **sample** — draw scenarios from the input
distribution and push each one through.  For a portfolio, "the input
distribution" means the **joint** distribution of all the assets at once, and
sampling it *jointly* is the whole game.  Get every marginal right but the
joint wrong and your scenarios will systematically miss the one event a
portfolio fears: the day everything falls together.

This page climbs a ladder of four scenario generators, in rising order of
honesty: **#1 independent → #2 Gaussian → #3 Student-t → #4 RBIG**.  Each
rung takes the same exam — *reproduce the co-crash, price the tail* — on Act
1's running character, the fat-tailed bank pair from the
[chapter opener](01-uncertainty-is-probability.qmd#two-questions-two-acts).

```{python}
#| label: load-character
# Act 1's running character: a fat-tailed pair whose worst days arrive together
a, b = datasets.tail_dependent_pair(n=2000, seed=0)
X = np.column_stack([a, b])                  # (n_days, 2)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
n_draw = 20_000                              # scenarios per generator
```

## The Target — VaR, the 1-in-100 Morning

Before grading generators, fix the quantity they must reproduce.
**Value at Risk** is a quantile of the portfolio's daily P&L — the loss that
a 1-in-100 morning meets or beats:

$$
\text{VaR}_{1\%} : \qquad \Pr\big[\,r_{\text{portfolio}} \le \text{VaR}_{1\%}\,\big] = 1\%.
$$

On the real 14-stock basket it looks like this:

```{python}
#| label: fig-var-target
#| fig-cap: "Daily returns of the equal-weight S&P basket (real data, 2007–2025). The 1% VaR is the quantile marking off the worst 1-in-100 mornings — the red sliver. A scenario generator is only as good as the tail of the scenarios it produces, because this is the part of the distribution it must price."
R = datasets.load_returns()                  # 14-stock daily returns DataFrame
port = R.mean(axis=1).to_numpy()             # equal-weight basket [daily return]
var_1pct = np.quantile(port, 0.01)           # the 1-in-100 morning

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 3.2))
bins = np.linspace(port.min(), port.max(), 120)
ax.hist(port[port > var_1pct], bins=bins, color=COOL, alpha=0.7)
ax.hist(port[port <= var_1pct], bins=bins, color=CRASH, alpha=0.9)
ax.axvline(var_1pct, color=CRASH, lw=2.5, ls="--")
ax.annotate(f"1% VaR = {var_1pct:.1%}\nthe 1-in-100 morning",
            (var_1pct, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.55),
            xytext=(-10, 0), textcoords="offset points", ha="right",
            fontsize=11, color=CRASH, fontweight="bold")
ax.set_xlabel("daily return — equal-weight S&P basket (real data)")
ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Alongside VaR we track a second exam question, borrowed straight from the
[dependence chapter](../dependence/index.qmd): the **co-crash rate** — given
that one asset is having a worst-5% day, how often is the other one too?
Under independence the answer is just 5% (knowing about the first tells you
nothing about the second); the real pair answers far higher, and a generator
that cannot reproduce the co-crash cannot price the joint tail.

## Rung 1 · Independent Resampling — Fails

The obvious move: resample each asset's own history, separately.

```{python}
#| label: indep-draws
# scenario = ( resample(a) , resample(b) ) — each column drawn on its own,
# i.e. sampling from p(a)·p(b): the dependence chapter's SHUFFLED REFERENCE
idx = rng.integers(0, len(a), size=(n_draw, 2))    # (n_draw, 2) day indices
indep_draws = np.column_stack([a[idx[:, 0]], b[idx[:, 1]]])
```

Every **marginal** is exactly right — by construction, each column is the
true history.  But the pairing of the columns is random, so the draws come
from the product $p(a)\,p(b)$.  That product is precisely the
[independence reference](../dependence/01-correlation.qmd#the-independence-reference)
the dependence chapter built by shuffling — the distribution that *defines*
"no dependence."  All the joint structure is destroyed before the first
scenario is drawn.

```{python}
#| label: fig-independent-fail
#| fig-cap: "Real pair vs independent resampling. The marginals are identical (each axis histograms the same history); the joint is unrecognizable. The diagonal smear into the lower-left corner — the days that hurt — is simply gone, and the co-crash rate collapses to the chance-level 5% that independence predicts."
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, D, col, name in [
    (axL, X, COOL,
     f"real · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(a, b, 0.05):.0%}"),
    (axR, indep_draws[:2000], CRASH,
     f"independent · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(indep_draws[:, 0], indep_draws[:, 1], 0.05):.1%}"),
]:
    ax.scatter(D[:, 0], D[:, 1], s=6, c=col, alpha=0.35, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlim(-5, 4); ax.set_ylim(-5, 4)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Independent resampling can never produce the co-crash — and the co-crash *is*
the risk.  Strike one, and a lesson: a generator is graded on its joint, not
its marginals.

## Rung 2 · Gaussian Monte-Carlo — Right Correlation, Wrong Extremes

Keep the co-movement: fit a mean and covariance, sample a multivariate
normal.

$$
x = \mu + L z, \qquad z \sim \mathcal N(0, I), \qquad L L^\top = \Sigma .
$$

```{python}
#| label: gauss-draws
def sample_gaussian(
    D: Float[Array, "n_days 2"], n: int, rng_: np.random.Generator
) -> Float[Array, "n 2"]:
    """Gaussian Monte-Carlo: x = μ + L·z with z ~ 𝒩(0, I) and L·Lᵀ = Σ.

    The Cholesky factor L 'colors' independent noise with the fitted
    covariance — linear co-movement in, nothing else.
    """
    μ = D.mean(axis=0)                       # (2,) sample mean   [return units]
    Σ = np.cov(D.T)                          # (2, 2) sample covariance
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(Σ)                # (2, 2) with L·Lᵀ = Σ
    z = rng_.normal(size=(n, 2))             # (n, 2) white noise ~ 𝒩(0, I)
    return μ + einx.dot("n d, k d -> n k", z, L)   # apply L to every draw


gauss_draws = sample_gaussian(X, n_draw, rng)
```

This captures **linear** co-movement — the cloud tilts correctly, the
correlation matrix is matched exactly.  But two things go quietly wrong in
the corner:

::: {.callout-note icon=false}
## Why Gaussian Tails Are Thin, Precisely
A Gaussian density decays like $e^{-x^2/2}$; a Student-$t$ decays only
polynomially, $\sim |x|^{-(\nu+1)}$.  Worse, the Gaussian *copula* has
**asymptotic tail independence**: the probability that both assets breach an
extreme quantile together $\to 0$ as the quantile deepens — *however high
the correlation*.  Matching the covariance is not matching the tail.  This
is the [Gaussian shadow](../dependence/03-mutual-information.qmd) of the
dependence chapter, met from the other direction.
:::

```{python}
#| label: fig-gauss-mc
#| fig-cap: "Left: the Gaussian Monte-Carlo cloud over the real pair — the bulk and the tilt are right, but the lower-left corner is empty. Right: push both scenario sets through the 50/50 portfolio and the Gaussian's loss histogram stops short; its 1% VaR is visibly too optimistic, exactly where it matters."
port_real = einx.mean("n d -> n", X)         # 50/50 portfolio, real days
port_gauss = einx.mean("n d -> n", gauss_draws)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
axL.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], s=6, c=COOL, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none",
            label="real")
axL.scatter(gauss_draws[:2000, 0], gauss_draws[:2000, 1], s=6, c=WARM,
            alpha=0.25, edgecolors="none", label="Gaussian MC")
axL.set_xlim(-5, 4); axL.set_ylim(-5, 4)
axL.set_xticks([]); axL.set_yticks([])
axL.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False, markerscale=2); despine(axL)

bins = np.linspace(min(port_real.min(), port_gauss.min()), 3, 60)
axR.hist(port_real, bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="real")
axR.hist(port_gauss, bins=bins, density=True, color=WARM, alpha=0.5,
         label="Gaussian MC")
axR.axvline(np.quantile(port_real, 0.01), color=COOL, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.axvline(np.quantile(port_gauss, 0.01), color=WARM, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.set_title(f"1% VaR · real {np.quantile(port_real, 0.01):.2f} "
              f"vs Gaussian {np.quantile(port_gauss, 0.01):.2f}", fontsize=12)
axR.set_yticks([]); axR.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False); despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Same cloud in the middle, **too-optimistic VaR** at the quantile the desk
actually reports.  Strike two — but a more instructive one: the failure is
not in the dependence *strength* (the correlation is perfect) but in the
dependence *shape*.

## Rung 3 · Student-t Monte-Carlo — Patch the Tails by Hand

If thin tails are the problem, the classic fix is to keep $\mu$ and $\Sigma$
and swap the bell for a fatter one:

$$
x = \mu + \frac{L z}{\sqrt{g/\nu}}, \qquad z \sim \mathcal N(0, I),
\quad g \sim \chi^2_\nu .
$$

Read the recipe: draw a Gaussian scenario, then divide by a *random scale*
$\sqrt{g/\nu}$.  Most days $g/\nu \approx 1$ and nothing changes; on the rare
day $g$ comes out small, **both** assets are amplified by the same shock —
which is exactly how real crises behave, and exactly what gives the Student-t
genuine *tail dependence* where the Gaussian has none.  One new knob, the
degrees of freedom $\nu$: smaller $\nu$, fatter tails, with
$\nu \to \infty$ recovering the Gaussian.

```{python}
#| label: t-draws
def fit_t_dof(D: Float[Array, "n_days 2"]) -> float:
    """Pick ν by maximum likelihood over a small grid.

    The multivariate-t with shape matrix S has covariance S·ν/(ν−2), so we
    scale S = Σ·(ν−2)/ν to keep the fitted covariance equal to the sample's.
    """
    μ, Σ = D.mean(axis=0), np.cov(D.T)
    ν_grid = (2.5, 3, 4, 5, 6, 8, 12)
    log_liks = [multivariate_t(μ, Σ * (ν - 2) / ν, df=ν).logpdf(D).sum()
                for ν in ν_grid]
    return ν_grid[int(np.argmax(log_liks))]


def sample_t(
    D: Float[Array, "n_days 2"], ν: float, n: int, rng_: np.random.Generator
) -> Float[Array, "n 2"]:
    """Student-t Monte-Carlo: x = μ + L·z / √(g/ν), one shared shock per day.

    g ~ χ²_ν is drawn ONCE per scenario and divides both assets — the shared
    shock is what creates tail dependence (a Gaussian has a shock per asset).
    """
    μ, Σ = D.mean(axis=0), np.cov(D.T)
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(Σ * (ν - 2) / ν)  # shape matrix → covariance Σ
    z = rng_.normal(size=(n, 2))             # (n, 2) white noise
    g = rng_.chisquare(ν, size=n)            # (n,) one scale shock per scenario
    colored = einx.dot("n d, k d -> n k", z, L)
    return μ + einx.divide("n d, n -> n d", colored, np.sqrt(g / ν))


ν_fit = fit_t_dof(X)
t_draws = sample_t(X, ν_fit, n_draw, rng)
print(f"fitted degrees of freedom: ν = {ν_fit:g}")
```

```{python}
#| label: fig-t-mc
#| fig-cap: "Student-t Monte-Carlo with the maximum-likelihood ν. Left: the scenario cloud now reaches into the joint lower-left corner. Right: the portfolio-loss tail and the 1% VaR land nearly on top of the real ones."
port_t = einx.mean("n d -> n", t_draws)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
axL.scatter(X[:, 0], X[:, 1], s=6, c=COOL, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none",
            label="real")
axL.scatter(t_draws[:2000, 0], t_draws[:2000, 1], s=6, c=PURPLE, alpha=0.25,
            edgecolors="none", label=f"Student-t (ν = {ν_fit:g})")
axL.set_xlim(-5, 4); axL.set_ylim(-5, 4)
axL.set_xticks([]); axL.set_yticks([])
axL.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False, markerscale=2); despine(axL)

bins = np.linspace(min(port_real.min(), port_t.min()), 3, 60)
axR.hist(port_real, bins=bins, density=True, color=COOL, alpha=0.55, label="real")
axR.hist(port_t, bins=bins, density=True, color=PURPLE, alpha=0.4,
         label="Student-t")
axR.axvline(np.quantile(port_real, 0.01), color=COOL, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.axvline(np.quantile(port_t, 0.01), color=PURPLE, lw=2, ls="--")
axR.set_title(f"1% VaR · real {np.quantile(port_real, 0.01):.2f} "
              f"vs Student-t {np.quantile(port_t, 0.01):.2f}", fontsize=12)
axR.set_yticks([]); axR.legend(fontsize=10, frameon=False); despine(axR)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The fitted $\nu$ brings the tail back to life — but read the fine print
before celebrating.  The shape is still **assumed**: symmetric (real crashes
are skewed — the down-tail is heavier than the up-tail), elliptical, one
global $\nu$ for every direction.  And this particular pair was
*manufactured* from a Student-t recipe, so the guessed family happens to be
exactly right.  **Hold that thought for the real-data exam below.**  This is
the [dependence chapter's fork](../dependence/05-gaussianization.qmd)
again: *assume* the shape — or *learn* it.

## Rung 4 · RBIG Backward — Learn the Joint, Then Invert

The top rung guesses nothing.  Recall the spine of the course:

$$
\underbrace{z = T(x)}_{\text{forward: measure / remove}}
\qquad\qquad
\underbrace{x = T^{-1}(z)}_{\text{backward: propagate}}
$$

[Gaussianization](../dependence/05-gaussianization.qmd) learned an invertible
map $T$ that turns the real, dependent, fat-tailed data into an independent
Gaussian ball — and *measured* dependence by what the map had to remove.
Run it **backward** and the same map is a scenario generator: draw
$z \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$ (trivial), invert ($x = T^{-1}(z)$), and out comes
a scenario from the *learned* joint — skew, fat tails, co-crash and all.
The change-of-variables formula is the warranty:
$p_X(x) = p_Z(T(x))\,\lvert\det J\rvert$, exactly.

```{python}
#| label: fig-rbig-scenarios
#| fig-cap: "RBIG run backward: fit the invertible map on the real pair, sample the Gaussian ball, invert. The generated scenarios reproduce the co-crash corner the Gaussian missed — without ever being told a parametric family."
rbig_draws = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(X).sample(n_draw)

fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for ax, D, col, name in [
    (axL, X, COOL,
     f"real · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(a, b, 0.05):.0%}"),
    (axR, rbig_draws[:2000], GREEN,
     f"RBIG · co-crash {cocrash_fraction(rbig_draws[:, 0], rbig_draws[:, 1], 0.05):.0%}"),
]:
    ax.scatter(D[:, 0], D[:, 1], s=6, c=col, alpha=0.3, edgecolors="none")
    ax.set_xlim(-5, 4); ax.set_ylim(-5, 4)
    ax.set_title(name, fontsize=12)
    ax.set_xticks([]); ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Learned joint, learned tails: the diagonal of joint crashes survives the
round-trip through Gaussian space.  The same tool that *measured* dependence
in the dependence chapter is, run in reverse, the only generator on the
ladder that never had to guess a shape.

## Every Generator, Same Exam

All four side by side, against the two exam questions:

```{python}
#| label: fig-generator-scorecard
#| fig-cap: "The ladder graded. Left: co-crash rate (the chance the second asset is in its worst 5% given the first is) — independent collapses to the 5% chance level, Gaussian undershoots, Student-t and RBIG match. Right: 1% VaR of the 50/50 portfolio — the Gaussian shaves the tail; the top two rungs price it. The dashed line is the real data's answer."
names = ["real\n(the data)", "#1\nindependent", "#2\nGaussian MC",
         "#3\nStudent-t", "#4\nRBIG"]
scenario_sets = [X, indep_draws, gauss_draws, t_draws, rbig_draws]
colors = [INK, CRASH, WARM, PURPLE, GREEN]

cocrash_rates = [cocrash_fraction(S[:, 0], S[:, 1], 0.05) for S in scenario_sets]
var_1pcts = [np.quantile(einx.mean("n d -> n", S), 0.01) for S in scenario_sets]

xs = np.arange(5)
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.6))
axL.bar(xs, cocrash_rates, 0.6, color=colors)
axL.axhline(cocrash_rates[0], color=INK, lw=1.4, ls="--")
axL.set_title("co-crash rate (both in worst 5%)", fontsize=12)
axR.bar(xs, var_1pcts, 0.6, color=colors)
axR.axhline(var_1pcts[0], color=INK, lw=1.4, ls="--")
axR.set_title("1% VaR of the 50/50 portfolio", fontsize=12)
for ax in (axL, axR):
    ax.set_xticks(xs); ax.set_xticklabels(names, fontsize=9)
    despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Independent fails both questions; Gaussian passes the first and shaves the
second.  Student-t nearly aces the exam — but remember, these banks were
*built* from a t, so its guess is exactly right.  RBIG gets to the same place
**with no guess at all**.  Whether that distinction matters is an empirical
question, so real data gets the final word.

## The Real-Data Exam — JPM & BAC

Same four generators, but the character is now real: JPMorgan and Bank of
America daily returns, 2007–2025.  What does the 1-in-100 morning cost a
50:50 holder?

```{python}
#| label: fig-real-exam
#| fig-cap: "The exam on real data. The Gaussian shaves a full point off the 1-in-100 morning. The Student-t — hero of the synthetic exam — does no better here: real crash days are skewed, and no symmetric bell can say so. RBIG, guessing nothing, wins back most of the gap."
X_real = R[["JPM", "BAC"]].to_numpy()        # (n_days, 2) real daily returns
rng_real = np.random.default_rng(0)

gauss_real = sample_gaussian(X_real, n_draw, rng_real)
ν_real = fit_t_dof(X_real)
t_real = sample_t(X_real, ν_real, n_draw, rng_real)
rbig_real = AnnealedRBIG(n_layers=30, random_state=0).fit(X_real).sample(n_draw)

names_real = ["real data", "Gaussian MC", f"Student-t (ν = {ν_real:g})", "RBIG"]
var_real = [np.quantile(einx.mean("n d -> n", S), 0.01)
            for S in (X_real, gauss_real, t_real, rbig_real)]
colors_real = [INK, WARM, PURPLE, GREEN]

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.4))
ax.bar(np.arange(4), var_real, 0.55, color=colors_real)
ax.axhline(var_real[0], color=INK, lw=1.4, ls="--")
for k, v in enumerate(var_real):
    ax.text(k, v / 2, f"{v:.1%}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=13,
            fontweight="bold", color="white")
ax.set_xticks(np.arange(4)); ax.set_xticklabels(names_real, fontsize=11)
ax.set_ylabel("1% VaR · JPM/BAC 50:50")
ax.set_yticks([]); despine(ax)
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

Three lessons in one bar chart:

1. **The Gaussian understates the worst mornings** — on real banks, by
   roughly a full percentage point of daily return.  At desk scale that is
   not a rounding error; it is the difference between surviving the week and
   explaining it to a regulator.
2. **A fatter assumed family is not the same as the right family.**  The
   Student-t aced the synthetic exam because the synthetic data *was* a t.
   On real returns its symmetric, elliptical shape buys almost nothing —
   real crashes are skewed, and no global $\nu$ can express "the down-tail
   is heavier than the up-tail."
3. **Learning the shape transfers; assuming it does not.**  RBIG never knew
   a family existed and recovers most of the gap on both datasets — the
   *assume vs learn* fork, settled by experiment.

::: {.eli5}
**One-liner recap.**  Independent sampling kills the joint; Gaussian
Monte-Carlo keeps the correlation but thins the tail; Student-t fattens the
tail but assumes its shape; RBIG (or a flow) run backward *learns* the joint
and keeps the real extremes — the only generator that never guessed.
:::

Act 1 sampled the *world*.  Act 2 turns to a single model and asks how wrong
its prediction is.  First, open the black box every prediction comes out of —
[the regression recipe](04-regression-recipe.qmd) — then put a band around it
in [predictive bands: noise & ensembles](05-predictive-bands.qmd).
